newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Republicans wrap up budget accord.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Republicans wrap up budget accord.

text.p: The White House and Republican leaders on Thursday wrapped up an agreement to balance the budget by 2002 and give most Americans a share in an $85 billion tax cut over the next five years.

President Bill Clinton was described as ecstatic to hear of the accord, which resolved deep disagreements that remained after the preliminary budget deal was announced with much fanfare on May 2. The budget was last balanced in 1969.

"He's ecstatic," White House legislative director John Hilley told reporters. "We got 98 percent of what we needed and wanted ... This will be a budget agreement that not only balances but, under current projections, drives us into surpluses in the second five years," he said.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, clearly relieved to have weeks of intense budget negotiations behind him, announced the agreement. "Yes, we have an agreement and we are not going to go through it again. It's over. We got it," the Mississippi Republican told reporters off the Senate floor.
But Democrats emerging from a briefing by White House staff remained noncommittal and said they wanted to see the written details.

"I think they have done a commendable job in pulling it all together," Representative John Spratt, chief Democrat on the Budget Committee, said. But he said they had to make sure the budget presented to Congress implements the agreement. "We aren't through," he added.

After the briefings for Democrats, Hilley said he expected "a very, very strong majority" of Senate Democrats would vote for it, but was less sure about the House. "I think we will have a majority in the House," he said.

The plan protects a list of domestic programmes in 13 areas -- including Head Start preschool education, bilingual and immigrant schooling, national parks operations and the Environmental Protection Agency operations. It won greater funding for disability benefits paid to legal immigrants.
But the administration will have to continue to fight for funds for two political hot buttons -- Clinton's AmeriCorps youth service and Goals 2000, an educational standards programme.

Republican leaders have put the budget on the express train for passage by the end of next week before Congress takes a one-week Memorial Day holiday. The House Budget Committee meets on it Friday, and the Senate panel Monday.
The budget forms the blueprint for tax and spending policies for the next five years and accounts for $9 trillion in government costs during the time.

It does not require Clinton's signature, but it was negotiated with him to ease passage of legislation that will enact the spending cuts needed to reduce the deficit to zero by 2002 and the tax cuts sought by both parties.

According to the congressional budget panels, this budget deal would result in an increase in the deficit next year to $90.2 billion from an expected $67 billion in the current fiscal 1997. It would start declining in fiscal 1999 and would hit a slight surplus of $1.2 billion in fiscal 2002. Hilley said it would lead to continuing surpluses through 2007.

As part of the final, and written, budget accord worked out in the past 13 days, Lott and House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich signed two letters spelling out the tax cut conditions and promising continued cooperation with the administration.

They removed an important bone of contention by clarifying that the president will win his long-sought HOPE scholarship programme to provide $35 billion worth of tax deductions and credits to help families pay for post-secondary education.

They also agreed that the tax cuts will not be permitted to explode in the years beyond 2002. There had been great concern that the capital gains tax cut, which Republicans called their "crown jewel," would lose much revenue. The total net tax cut will be capped at $250 billion through 2007.
The tax cut letter spells out as priorities a broad-based permanent capital gains tax cut, relief from inheritance taxes, a $500 per child tax credit and expansion of individual retirement accounts.

Lott said the budget deal also includes an automatic extension in the U.S. debt ceiling to provide enough authority to carry the government's borrowing needs through Dec. 15, 1999. This change takes the contentious debt ceiling increase out of the politics of the 1998 election.

The budget cuts Medicare health care spending by $115 billion over five years, cuts Medicaid by $16 billion and gives the president $31.7 billion for his new domestic policy initiatives. While government spending would go up over the five years, the increase would be about $141 billion less than under current policies.

White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles, Office of Management and Budget director Franklin Raines and other top White House officials had been closeted with Republican leaders most of the day in Gingrich's office, working out last minute snags. The May 2 agreement carried only verbal promises and was then open to dispute.
